column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The source places the quarries on the south-west coast of Euboea between Styra and Karystos; the entry says near Karystos in southern Euboea, which agrees. The source lists Westminster Abbey and Saint Mark's under the Byzantine-period reuse without saying whether the stone was newly quarried or reused material; worded as 'used'.

The entry says he fled the French revolutionary armies in 1794; the source does not mention the flight, so it is not told here. The source lists him as Prince-Bishop of Augsburg until 1812 although the prince-bishopric was secularised in 1803; the text says only that the prince-bishopric was secularised.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words, most of it a quotation about the Phocaeans; it adds little beyond the entry (and dates the voyage c. 640 BC against the entry's c. 638 BCE)
All of this is literary tradition; the text attributes each episode to its source. The source spells the hero both Cúchulainn and Cú Chulainn; Cúchulainn used.
The source gives the surrender as 2 October 1932 but also counts '87 days of fighting (July 9 to October 4)'; the text uses the surrender date only and gives no count of days.
The entry mentions the Tallinn Manual, which the source does not; it is not told here.

The source says the meetings summoned by the kings began in 1162; the entry says the Cortes met from the thirteenth century. Neither date is given in the text. The source is mostly about the modern regional parliament; the early Cortes section is short, so the text is near the minimum length.

The source's lead says the council was established in 1480 under Isabella I, while its history section gives John I's creation in 1385 and the 1480 reform, as the entry does; the text follows the latter. The source dates the Council of the Indies' split only as '1 August' within 1522-1524, so no date is given.
The source calls Couserans a former county and says Saint-Lizier lost its see at the time of the French Revolution; the entry gives 1801. No year is given in the text.

The entry says Invergordon was an important naval base in both world wars; the source says only that it was at one time a major Home Fleet base and describes the World War II seaplane base, so no war is named for the naval base.

The source calls the Corpus Christi series the work of an anonymous late-17th-century painter, which some researchers attribute to the workshops of Diego Quispe Tito and Pumacallao; the attribution is left out.
The source is short (about 380 words); the text uses nearly all of it. It does not mention the fortress of Buyeo or the date of surrender given in the entry.
The source gives the length as 1,287 km; the entry says about 1,290 km. The total is not repeated in the text. The source dates the Mbacké and Touba branch to around 1931 to 1933 (sources differ).
The source is short and says nothing of Western learning, Takano Choei, Murata Zoroku or the steamship named in the entry; none of that is told here. The text uses nearly all the source's facts.

The source is mainly about the modern town. It does not name Henry III as the castle's builder, nor the Mercian destruction of 822 or the Mediterranean pottery; none of these is told here. It spells the prince both Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and ap Gruffydd; the first is used.

The source says recent scholarship has shown it likely that both hymns were written for the Pythaids of 128 BC, while the First Hymn was long dated c. 138 BC; the text keeps that hedge, as the entry's dates line does.

The source says that in 1042 he claimed the kingship of Leinster and installed his son Murchad as King of Dublin; the entry dates the taking of Dublin to 1052. No year is given for either in the text.

The source says he and Pedro Calungsod were killed by Matå'pang and Hurao; the entry says he was killed by a Chamorro chief. The killers are not named in the text. The source quotes two different figures for the 1710 census (3,197 from Wiecko; 3,539 'most commonly cited' from Goetzfridt), so no figure is given.

The entry says she abdicated for her son in 1867; the article gives her first reign as 1842-1865 and her son Mohamed as sultan 1865-1874. Date of abdication left out. The article gives her restoration as 1874 in the lead but says 'When the French returned in 1871, she was restored'; left undated. The article says Griffiths returned in 1841 and found the daughter on the throne, but also that her father died in 1842; left out. Entry dates birth 1836/37, article c. 1837; birth year not given in the text.

The article says Santana had wrested the presidency from Báez; the entry does not mention Santana. The article puts O'Donnell's fall in 1866, after the annulment; left out as it reads oddly in sequence. Casualty totals vary in the article (over 10,000 casualties; New York Times: more than 12,000 dead); only the March 1864 figure is given.
Short article; text kept to what it gives. The entry says the cathedral town of Dornoch stands on the northern shore; the article does not mention it.
The entry dates the abduction of Derbforgaill/Devorgilla to 1152; the article says 1153. Year left out. The 2009-2015 story of the abandoned Abbey Manor hotel left out as passing news.
The article does not mention 1907 or Ugyen Wangchuck; the entry's end date is not contradicted.
The article gives no year for the 3rd Duke's sale of Manx sovereignty; the entry's 1765 is not contradicted and not repeated. Living holders (12th Duke, heir) not named.
Article: abandoned Baku on the night of 14/15 September; entry: withdrew on 14 September. Exact date of departure left out.

The article names the scholars (Rose, Mayor, Rostovtzeff, Kersley, Mommsen) by surname only; surnames kept. One passage of the article calls her father Pharnaces I; elsewhere Pharnaces II. Only Pharnaces II used. The article also mentions the alternative that she died in 14 BCE and Polemon ruled to 8 BCE; left out, as the entry dates her death c. 8 CE.
SKIPPED: article has under 400 words, most of it already in the entry; a longer text would be padded

The article gives the killings variously as 1755-1757, 1755-1758 and a campaign of 1757-58; dates beyond the entry's 1755 start left out of the text. Death estimates vary (420,000-480,000; 600,000-800,000 population); only Wei Yuan's figures given.

The entry says small princely states and estates were absorbed into East Punjab; the article says the princely states were combined into PEPSU, a separate union, merged into Punjab only in 1956. The text says PEPSU was separate, which the entry does not deny outright, but the editor may wish to check the entry's sentence.

The article gives the autobiography's publication as 1976 in Honours and 1978 in the works list; no year given. The article spells the medal 'Edward Ullendorf Medal' (one f) once; I used the double-f spelling of his name - editor may check.

The article calls L'Egyptienne fortnightly in one place and monthly in another; frequency left out. The article says Hawaa was 'the EFU's second journal' though dated 1954-1969, after the union's dissolution; given only as a journal she edited.
The article's lead also says the CIA tried to suppress the book through front organisations, in an unfinished sentence without detail; left out.
The entry dates Mateus's mission to around 1509; the article gives no year, so none is given.
The article says Qianfei was assassinated in January 466 but also places the killing in winter 465; no date given for his accession.
The entry dates his birth to 467; the article gives 8 August 469, while its own family list under Emperor Ming gives 467-479. Birth date and his ages (given as 10 in 477 and 12 in 479) left out.
The article says the Book of Wei's description is 'highly suspect'; I attributed the suspicion to historians - the article does not name who holds it. Editor may reword.

Article: died 3 February 535, 'around the new year 535', poison 'in all likelihood' placed by Yuwen's assassins; entry says Yuwen 'had him poisoned early in 535'. Kept the article's hedge without contradicting the entry. Article spells 'secret edits'; written as edicts.

Entry says Respected for political wisdom; did not repeat. Marriage March/April 1625 per article, consistent with entry's 1625; not restated. Article: Oboi lured into a trap (forced to sit on a broken chair) - detail left out.
SKIPPED: article of about 330 words, almost all of it on the coins, which the entry already describes in full

Article gives death as 693; entry says 'around 693' - year omitted in my text. Article quotes an ancient epitaph saying he was bishop for eleven years, which conflicts with 675-693 in both article and entry: left out. Left out the recent Soulton Hall relic thesis (speculative).

Article gives 40 mu as about 1.1 hectares in one place and about 2.6 hectares in another: no conversion given. Article credits the Taika reforms to Prince Shotoku Taishi; left out the name as doubtful.
SKIPPED: article of about 250 words; too little beyond the entry for a longer text

Article says Faisal appointed Abdullah bin Rashid Amir of Ha'il in 1835; entry says the taking of Ha'il was in 1836. Left the date out. Article says he was forced into exile 'by the Ottomans' who sent an expedition, while also naming Egyptian forces and the Egyptian governor; entry says an Egyptian expedition. Wrote Egyptian. Mesaimeer payment given as 4,000 German krones in the article: amount omitted.
SKIPPED: article of about 300 words, mostly dimensions and a 2026 damage report; too little for a longer text Article says the castle was damaged by US strikes on 8 March 2026; not used.

Article dates the compilation both 'in the late 1672' and 'eight years between 1664 and 1672'; used 1664-1672. Entry says late seventeenth century. Article's claim about a contribution to Bengal's proto-industrialisation is garbled; left out.

Article says the territory was granted to Calvert in 1620 and gives no founding year for the colony; entry says founded 1621. No founding year given in my text. Calvert's visits of 1627-1628 are not in the article.

Article dates the Kazakh famine 1932–1933 in its lead; entry says 1930–1933. No dates given for the famine in my text. Death toll figures vary in the article (1.5 million; 1-2 million; 1-2.3 million; 3 million by Abzhanov); gave the common range with attribution of higher estimates. Left out Yezhov's interrogation confession about their relationship.
Article lists 969 rocket arrows as invented by Yue Yifang and Feng Jisheng in its timeline but disputes this in its Rocket invention section; given only as the History of Song's attribution.

Article's lead names General Alfred-Amédée Dodds as French commander, but its body names Colonel Terrillon; Dodds is usually associated with the second war. Dodds left out. Article spells the second battle Atchoukpa; entry Atchoupa.

Article's casualty figures conflict (it says all women and children were killed, yet gives estimates from 69 dead to 1,500 killed, wounded or captured); gave only the attributed range. Article says troops camped southeast in one place and southwest in another; direction omitted.
Second wife in 1560 not named in the article.

Article places the execution in the centre square of Port-au-Prince; left the place out (doubtful). Article dates Assam's confession and his capture to 1758 while giving his death as 20 January 1758; sequence given without year beyond the execution date.
SKIPPED: article of about 300 words, mostly the campaigns the entry already names; it also gives his birth as 1748 against the entry's 1753 Article: born 1748; entry: 1753.

The entry says Jayachandra was defeated and killed by Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor; the article's lead names the Ghurid army under Qutbuddin Aibak, its History section Muhammad of Ghor and Qutbuddin Aibak. Left out who led the army. The article gives Chandradeva's independence as 'sometime before 1090' (lead) and 'before 1089' (Origin section).
The article spells the cave both Vijjadhara Guha and Vidyadhara Guha; the text uses Vijjadhara Guha throughout.

The article says he was seventy-one when he volunteered in 1018, which does not fit a birth in 948 by Western reckoning (probably Korean age). Age left out. The article spells the Liao general both Xiao Paiya (993) and Xiao Baiya (1018); kept as given for each campaign.

Article: in Mughal packs the reversed suits are bills, red gold coins, cloth and harps in India. Detail kept general. The entry says Ganjifa was introduced to India from Persia; the article reports this as believed, and also von Leyden's suggestion that the first Mughals brought it from Inner Asia. Not discussed.

The entry speaks of parts of Limburg; the article calls the 19th-century term Staats-Limburg historically incorrect and names the land States' Overmaas. The text uses Overmaas and does not dispute the entry's wording.
James Craig, named in the entry, is not in the article; not mentioned.

The entry says later kings 'such as Constantine III' continued his expansion; the article makes Constantine III (r. 894–923) his predecessor. Constantine III not named in the text: the entry's description may need correcting. The article calls Bagrat both his half-brother (lead) and his youngest brother (Life section); written as 'his brother'. Sons who reigned: Leon III (960–969), Demetrius III (969–976), Theodosius III (975–978).
The article gives no birth date; he was twelve on his father's death in 1672.
The article's lead says he ruled until his suicide; its body says possibly by suicide. Hedged.

The article dates Level VI.I both 3200–3000 BC and (by the excavator) c. 3500–3200 BC; the text says late fourth millennium only. The lead says the site was abandoned at the end of the 2nd millennium BC after an earthquake; Level III says abandoned near 1400 BC. Earthquake left out. The entry calls the Iron Age manor Median; the article does not use the word. Not repeated.
The article spells the Grand Master both Herman of Salza and Hermann von Salza; the text uses Herman of Salza and Salza.

The article lists Pomerania as well as Pomerelia among Poland's claims; only Pomerelia and the Chełmno Land named. The article mentions a 'Battle of Marienburg' before the treaty without describing it; left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (261 words in all); it adds only the Goguryeo campaigns of 204 and 209 and his succession by Gongsun Gong
The article's lead says Gongyang scholarship was revived in the late Ming dynasty; its later section describes the revival under the Qing. Only the Qing revival is told.

The entry says Goryeo retained land south of the Yalu in 993; the article says it formally incorporated land up to the Yalu then held by Jurchens. Worded neutrally. The article's relations section has Hyeonjong ordering war preparations next to the events of 942, which cannot be right; left out. The entry names the capital Kaesong; the article does not name it here.

The article calls Bachelet 'the former president' for a statement of 2009, when she was in office; her title left out. Article attributes a quotation to 'the former vocalist of Maná' in the Voces Unidas section, which is muddled (Cuevas was of La Ley); not used.

The entry says Sucre defeated the Peruvian army under La Mar at Tarqui; the article says only a Peruvian advance guard of 900 was beaten by more than 4,500 Gran Colombians, the bulk of the Peruvian army withdrew in order and the result was not decisive. The outcome of the battle is left out of the text. The entry names the Treaty of Guayaquil; the article calls the peace of 22 September 1829 the Larrea-Gual (Gual-Larrea) Treaty and does not say where it was signed. Treaty not named in the text. The article gives Bolívar's resolve to declare war as 3 June 1828 and the declaration as 3 July 1828; only 3 July used.

The article gives the Qing side in the Revolt of the Three Feudatories both as 400,000 Green Standard and 200,000 Bannermen and as 400,000 and 150,000, and elsewhere as an army of more than 900,000 non-Banner Han Chinese; only the 400,000 used.

The entry says they served until the frontier was abolished in 1881; the article says Grenz infantry remained in Austrian and Austro-Hungarian service until the First World War. End date left out of the text. The entry speaks of freedom from serfdom and religious tolerance; the article does not mention them.

The article dates the cashel to the sixth or seventh century (lead), probably the eighth century (description) and gives Lacy's link to 789; only 'second half of the first millennium' used, as in its chronology section. The entry says the ringfort was heavily reconstructed in the 1870s; the article gives the work as 1835–1874 and 'substantial restoration' in 1870. The text says only 'in the 19th century'.
The article gives his death as 16 March 255, consistent with the entry; the day was left out.
Final accord date 29 December 1996 omitted as the entry gives December 1996 already.

The article says his death is disputed (official suicide in Paderborn vs killing by Luxembourgers); the entry says 'died in British custody, apparently by suicide'. Both versions are given here attributed; the unofficial versions place the killing during or after handover, which may sit uneasily with 'in British custody' - editor may wish to drop the second paragraph of the last section.

The article says construction of the Divine Bell 'began in 742 and finished during the reign of King Hyoseong' - impossible, as Hyoseong preceded Gyeongdeok (the bell was finished under Hyegong); the bell's dates were left out. The entry says only that the bell was begun in his reign. Article gives his birth as 723~724.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, and its dates (death August 1029, independence 1014) differ from the entry's (d. 1028, 1015) Article: died August 1029; ruled 1014-1029; declared independence and recognised the Abbasids in 1014; ceasefire 1016, Zirid recognition 1018. Entry: d. 1028, break in 1015. One of the two needs checking.

Article: the cathedral was completed in 1201 after Zakare bought Harich; the entry says the monastery was enlarged after 1201, when the Zakarids acquired it and built the church. The completion year was left out to avoid contradicting the entry.

The entry states that the inscription records the recovery of a Jain image taken by a Nanda king; the article reports this as one reading (Glasenapp, Rao, Thapar) and gives Sonya Quintanilla's objection that it was not an image. To avoid contradicting the entry, the point was left out. Article spells the name Buhler; written Bühler - may be flagged.
The article gives the founding as 23 April 1633 in its lead and 27 April 1633 later; the day was left out (the entry says April 1633). It also places Nördlingen in November 1634; month left out.
Article says he was imprisoned 'for about six months'; the entry says 'for months' - consistent.
Article dates his rule of Wrocław from 1296, with his brothers as co-rulers until 1311; the entry says from 1311. Written so as not to give a starting year beyond the 1311 division.

Article gives his death as 1274 in the lead but says he was captured and hanged within a year of 1272; the entry has d. 1273. Year left out. Article dates the victory at Pokarwis to 21 January 1261; the entry says 1260. Pokarwis left out of the text.

Article: Bopearachchi dates him c. 90-70 BC, R. C. Senior c. 95-80 BC, and the Chinese records, if they concern him, would put his reign's end around 40 BC. The entry has fl. c. 90-70 BCE, so the alternative dates were left out.
The article dates him only as fl. c. 1468 - c. 1504 and gives no date for the Tallinn altar; the entry's c. 1430 birth and 1481 completion are not in the article and were not repeated.

The article dates the princely title to 17 October 1623 in its History section and to 1624 in the section on Zdeněk Vojtěch; the entry says 1624. The year was left out. The 4th Prince's death is given as 1737 in the list and 1734 in his paragraph; not used.

Article title spells the name Sharvashidze; the entry Shervashidze. The text uses Sharvashidze for individuals as the article does. Article says nothing of the Dadiani of Mingrelia (the entry's claim).

The article gives the river as Uyu in the lead and Uru later; both forms used as the article does. Left out: the KIA's killing of addicts and dealers (told without attribution in the article) and the smaller disasters of 2008, 2009, 2018, 2019 and 2021.

The article gives the raising of the Shwedagon Pagoda as April 1775 in its lead and 1774 in its Culture section; no year printed. The article dates his first invasion of Ayutthaya to 1765 and the sack to 1767; the entry's 1767 sack is consistent and not repeated.

The article estimates over 130 million adobe bricks and calls it the largest pre-Columbian adobe structure in the Americas; the entry says an estimated hundred million and one of the largest. Neither figure printed. A short article (about 330 words of substance), much of it already in the entry; the text is near the minimum length.

The article gives his death as 27 July 1101 in its lead and as 17 July 1101 (four days after becoming a monk on 13 July) in its body; no day of death printed, only 'four days later'. The entry's refoundation date of St Werburgh's (1093) is not in the article; not repeated.

The entry says the Dauphiné passed in 1349 to the king's eldest son; the article says the final agreement of 1349 named the king's grandson Charles, who became the first Valois dauphin, after a 1344 arrangement that had named the king's eldest son John. The recipient of 1349 is not named in the text. The university of Grenoble (1339) is not in the article.

The article spells the type both Furman-jog and Firman-jog; Firman-jog used. It spells the jokhim type both Jokhami and Jokhim. Left out the article's present-day remark that banks and insurers refuse jokhim hundis.
Short article; text near the minimum length.
Desc says he served the Hafsids after Valencia fell in 1238; the article has him settling in Tunis in 1240 after fleeing to Dénia and Murcia; consistent.
Short article; the Ricote valley and the fall of Córdoba in 1236 are in the entry and not repeated.
The article says that from 1216/17 he transposed the Čahār maqāla material; the entry dates the writing of the history to around 1216–1217. Consistent; no year repeated.
The entry names the Treaty of Kurakchay; the article only speaks of an agreement of 26 May 1805. Not named here. The article gives no year for his accession; the entry's 1763 is not repeated.

The article dates his rule from 1886 or 1887 to his death in 1933, his father's death to 1888 and his accession to 1895; the entry says he ruled from the late 1880s until 1931. No dates of reign printed. The entry dates the script to around 1896; the article says the work began at the turn of the 20th century. No start year printed. The entry describes a religion blending Islam, Christianity and local belief; the article says his syncretic religion drew on Christianity and Bamum religion before he converted to Islam. The syncretic religion is not described here.

The article says he founded the monastery in the 6th century; the entry dates him to around 500. No century of the founding printed. The article also lists Saint Patrick among his pupils; left out as chronologically doubtful and not needed. Legend that he was buried west of Brecon left out.
The article says the Japanese legation members were rescued three days later; not printed. Desc's 'July 1882' consistent with 23 July.

The entry calls them meetings in London; the article says the 1894 and 1932 conferences were held in Ottawa. The place of the 1932 conference is not printed. Short article; text near the minimum length.
Short article; text near the minimum length. The entry's 'usually counted as an early Lakhmid ruler' and the article's 'second Lakhmid king' agree.

The article gives both 'ten linguistic families with at least 78 distinct languages' and 'approximately 100 distinct languages'; no count of languages printed. The article gives the population at the end of the 19th century as both about 15,000 and 16,000; not printed.

The article says the Institutes was largely unknown in the West; the entry says it shaped later European legal traditions. Neither point printed. Left out Samuel Parsons Scott's poorly received translation.
Desc covers the 1416 rediscovery and the Renaissance; this adds the circumstances from the article.

The article dates the house arrest of Mousavi and Karroubi both to 2010 and to 2011; no year printed. The article gives Ashura as 7 December, the same date it gives National Students Day; no date printed for Ashura. The article dates Rouhani's campaign to 2014 in one place and gives campaigns of 2013 and 2017 in another; no year printed. Left out: the claim that the leaders remain under house arrest 'to this day'.
Short article; text near the minimum length. The entry's Xuanzang reference is not in the article.

The article says the chronology is uncertain: either c. 625-643 (after Euselnus) or 620-637 (after Eleutherius). The entry gives 625-643; I left the term's dates out. The entry dates the Lateran plunder to 640; the article gives no year for it (only 638 for Heraclius's demand to Severinus). Left undated. The entry says the sarcophagus is in San Vitale, Ravenna; the article places it in the Sancta Sanctorum. I left the location out.

The article does not give the 545 national history or Sadaham's role in the Daegaya conquest, nor the year of that conquest (the entry gives 562); I gave no year for Daegaya. The research-ship paragraph reports the article's sentence on the Japanese instruction without date; it touches the Ulleungdo/Dokdo dispute, so the editor may prefer to drop it.

The article implies the Tripartitum was written after his retirement and Szapolyai's election (i.e. after 1526), yet cites the 1517 Singrenius print; the entry says it was presented to the diet in 1514. I gave only the 1517 printing and no sequence. The entry's appointment as chief judge in Ottoman Buda is not in the article; not repeated. Birth year given as 1458? in the article; the entry has c. 1458. Not used.

The article's lead lists all five powers as parties on 30 August 1454 but then says the Pope and Alfonso acceded on 2 March 1455; the entry says the league was concluded by Venice, Milan and Florence and joined by the Papacy and Naples. I named no parties for 30 August.

The article dates My Father and Myself to 1968 in the works list and to 1969 in the section on his father; I gave no year. The article says he spent about five months in India; the entry says several months in 1923. Left without a figure.
The entry places the pass on the Czech-Slovak border; the article places it in a Czech municipality near the borders with Poland and Slovakia. I gave only the municipality.
The entry says he died in exile; the article says he died at Wołów, which he held as a lifelong fief from 1497. I gave the place without calling it exile or not.
The article distinguishes Queen Tribhuwaneswari (Kertanegara's eldest daughter) from Queen regnant Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi; the entry's Queen Tribhuwana is the former.
Left out the present (70th) Je Khenpo, a living person.

The article calls him approaching 70 at his election, which does not fit its birth year 1780 (the entry's too); left out. The article places the Piquet Revolt of 1844 in the paragraph about his service under Christophe; I put it after the Boyer years, as the date requires. The entry's suppression of peasant revolts in the south is not in the article.
The article gives his birth as 1534/1536; the entry has 1536. Not used. The article dates the Sancerre book 1574 in the text and 1573 in the works list; I gave no year.

The entry says an explosion destroyed the Dutch fort at Tobago in 1677; the article does not mention it. The entry says most of his squadron was wrecked; the article says nine ships were lost, half his fleet. I gave the counts only, not a share.

The article dates Jiaozhi's absorption into the Annan Protectorate to 679 in the lead and the Six Dynasties section, and to 670 in the Nanyue section; I wrote 'in the 670s'. The article says Nanyue first set up the Jiaozhi Commandery; the entry says it was a commandery under the Han after 111 BCE. Both are told without conflict. The Ming province's dates (1407-1427 in the entry) are not given in the article; not repeated.
The article calls Fulda the capital of the Electorate of Hesse, which is anachronistic for 1700; left out.
The entry's statement that the Old House of Lüneburg ruled until 1369 is not in the article; not repeated.

The article dates the father's death and the division of Nassau to 1606; the entry dates the division to 1607. The year is left out. The article gives no year for his elevation to prince; the entry's 1650 stands.
The quotations in the article are from Josephus but the article does not name him as their source; the text says only 'the ancient account'.
The article has little on his life; about 260 words is all it supports.
The article gives no end date for his chairmanship of the Executive Commission; the entry's 1942-1943 stands.
The article dates the arrest to AD 78; the entry gives his death as 79 CE after nine years in hiding. The arrest year is left out.

The article says the layers had been heavily reduced by the Kamakura period and, elsewhere, considerably reduced by the Muromachi period; neither period is named in the text, the entry already giving the Kamakura reduction.

The article dates the missionaries' arrival to 1822 and has Kaʻahumanu declaring Christianity the state religion in 1823 but baptised in 1825, and proclaiming laws eleven years after the missionaries arrived; these points are confused and left out.
The entry dates Treaty 7 to 1877; the article gives no year. Reserve population (4,570) left out as undated.
The article says the Portuguese 'occupied Kanara from 1498–1763'; left out as doubtful and unsupported elsewhere in the article.
The entry calls Karatay an emir, the article a vizier; both stand as titles, no contradiction.

The article's claim that the Karen conflict is the second-longest internal war after the Dagohoy rebellion is garbled in the text and left out. Brigade 5 killing ten soldiers is from the article; the entry's 'January 1949' is matched by 'early in 1949'.
SKIPPED: wrong article: the entry is Karyes on Mount Athos, the saved article is the village of Karyes in Laconia, Peloponnese
The founding story is a traditional account; the article gives no dates for it.
The article dates her husband's death and the start of her reign to 1672 and its end to 1697; the entry gives 1671 and her death in 1696. Neither year is printed; '25 years' agrees with both.

The article says the party dominated Thai politics for two decades and was dissolved in 1947; the entry gives 1927-1933 and fifteen years of dominance. The span and the year of dissolution are left out.
The article dates the passing of the Guaramid lands to the Bagrationi to c. 786; the entry says the Bagratids were based there from the early 9th century. The year is left out.
The entry already summarises the four sections in one sentence; this text sets out what each holds.

The article has a heading for the fort but no text under it, and nothing on the Reddi kings or the British named in the entry; the history in this text is limited to the 18th-century name. Industrial details kept to lasting facts.
The article says the programme was officially approved in Košice on 5 April but in fact signed in Moscow on 29 March; the entry says proclaimed on 5 April, which the text does not contradict.

The entry says he united Vengi with the Chola realm on taking the Chola throne; the article says he let his uncle Vijayaditya keep ruling Vengi after he became Chola emperor (and also that he was Eastern Chalukya monarch from 1061 to 1118). Both points left out.
The article also says the fisheries department set up a station on the Ing River in 1935 and made a dam; left out beside the 1939-1941 floodgate to avoid an unclear double account.
The entry dates the Burman settlement to the 9th century; the article says the first Myanmar probably settled about 800 and gives Luce's migration in the 8th century. Dates left out of the text.
The entry says she restored Naranjo's royal dynasty; the article says she came to establish a new dynasty. The text speaks only of the marriage and leaves the point out.
